claim: ERK3 controls IL-8 production and chemotaxis.
source: We have previously shown that ERK3, an atypical MAPK, controls IL-8 production and chemotaxis (Bogueka et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Bogueka et al., 2020).

claim: ERK3 directly acts as a guanine nucleotide exchange factor for CDC42.
source: Here, we show in human cells that ERK3 directly acts as a guanine nucleotide exchange factor for CDC42
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 3.

claim: ERK3 phosphorylates the ARP3 subunit of the ARP2/3 complex at S418.
source: ERK3 directly acts as a guanine nucleotide exchange factor for CDC42 and phosphorylates the ARP3 subunit of the ARP2/3 complex at S418 to promote filopodia formation and actin polymerization, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mass spectrometry and in vitro kinase assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: Depletion of ERK3 prevented both basal and EGF-dependent RAC1 and CDC42 activation.
source: Consistently, depletion of ERK3 prevented both basal and EGF-dependent RAC1 and CDC42 activation, maintenance of F-actin content, filopodia formation, and epithelial cell migration.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from pull-down assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: Depletion of ERK3 prevented maintenance of F-actin content.
source: Consistently, depletion of ERK3 prevented both basal and EGF-dependent RAC1 and CDC42 activation, maintenance of F-actin content, filopodia formation, and epithelial cell migration.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from F/G-actin assays shown in Figure 5.

claim: Depletion of ERK3 prevented filopodia formation.
source: Consistently, depletion of ERK3 prevented both basal and EGF-dependent RAC1 and CDC42 activation, maintenance of F-actin content, filopodia formation, and epithelial cell migration.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from confocal and SEM imaging shown in Figure 1.

claim: Depletion of ERK3 prevented epithelial cell migration.
source: Consistently, depletion of ERK3 prevented both basal and EGF-dependent RAC1 and CDC42 activation, maintenance of F-actin content, filopodia formation, and epithelial cell migration.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from cell tracking and migration assays shown in Figure 1.

claim: ERK3 protein bound directly to the purified ARP2/3 complex.
source: Further, ERK3 protein bound directly to the purified ARP2/3 complex and augmented polymerization of actin in vitro.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from GST pull-down and ELISA assays shown in Figure 6.

claim: ERK3 augmented polymerization of actin in vitro.
source: Further, ERK3 protein bound directly to the purified ARP2/3 complex and augmented polymerization of actin in vitro.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from pyrene-actin polymerization assays shown in Figure 5F.

claim: ERK3 kinase activity was required for the formation of actin-rich protrusions in mammalian cells.
source: ERK3 kinase activity was required for the formation of actin-rich protrusions in mammalian cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from complementation experiments with kinase-dead ERK3 shown in Figure 7.

claim: Actin is one of the most abundant and highly conserved proteins with over 95% homology among all isoforms.
source: Actin is one of the most abundant and highly conserved proteins with over 95% homology among all isoforms (Vandekerckhove and Weber, 1979).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vandekerckhove and Weber, 1979.

claim: In cells, actin is present in globular/monomeric form (G-actin), which can polymerize into branched and elongated filamentous forms (F-actin).
source: In cells, it is present in globular/monomeric form (G-actin), which can polymerize into branched and elongated filamentous forms (F-actin) in a dynamic, spatially, and temporally controlled process (Skruber et al., 2018; Lee and Dominguez, 2010; Carlsson, 2006; Carlier et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The cytoplasmic actin network regulates velocity and directionality of cell migration.
source: It regulates velocity and directionality of cell migration, enables intracellular signaling and transport, supports cell division, and more (Yamaguchi and Condeelis, 2007; dos Remedios et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yamaguchi and Condeelis, 2007 and dos Remedios et al., 2003.

claim: The actin cytoskeleton can form unique structures such as lamellipodia and filopodia.
source: Moreover, by branching and bundling of F-actin filaments the actin cytoskeleton can form unique structures such as lamellipodia and filopodia, which in epithelial cells regulate cell polarization and are crucial for the contact with their environment, while in other cell types these actin rich structures control motility, chemotaxis, and haptotaxis (Vasioukhin et al., 2000; Raich et al., 1999; Millard and Martin, 2008; Khurana and George, 2011; Bahri et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: The spatiotemporally defined branching and elongation of the polymerized actin filaments is achieved by activation of nucleation factors including the ARP2/3 complex, formins, and spire.
source: The spatiotemporally defined branching and elongation of the polymerized actin filaments is achieved by activation of nucleation factors including the Actin-related protein 2 and 3 (ARP2/3) complex, formins, and spire (Rouiller et al., 2008; Rohatgi et al., 1999; Carlier et al., 1999; Chesarone and Goode, 2009; Campellone and Welch, 2010; Pollard, 2007; Schuldt, 2005; Buracco et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: ARP2/3-dependent actin polymerization generates branched F-actin network.
source: It is well established that ARP2/3-dependent actin polymerization generates branched F-actin network, while formins generate unbranched filaments and promote growth of actin filaments at the barbed end (Pollard, 2007; Wood and Martin, 2002; Yang and Svitkina, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pollard, 2007; Wood and Martin, 2002; Yang and Svitkina, 2011.

claim: Formins generate unbranched filaments and promote growth of actin filaments at the barbed end.
source: It is well established that ARP2/3-dependent actin polymerization generates branched F-actin network, while formins generate unbranched filaments and promote growth of actin filaments at the barbed end (Pollard, 2007; Wood and Martin, 2002; Yang and Svitkina, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pollard, 2007; Wood and Martin, 2002; Yang and Svitkina, 2011.

claim: ARP2/3 complex is a major and highly conserved actin nucleator composed of seven subunits.
source: ARP2/3 complex is a major and highly conserved actin nucleator composed of seven subunits (Robinson et al., 2001; Goley and Welch, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Robinson et al., 2001 and Goley and Welch, 2006.

claim: The activation of ARP2/3 complex relies on binding to pre-formed actin filament and nucleation-promoting factors (NPFs).
source: The structural and biochemical properties of the ARP2/3 complex have been intensively studied in vitro, and apart from ATP, its activation relies on binding to pre-formed actin filament and nucleation-promoting factors (NPFs) (Robinson et al., 2001; Goley and Welch, 2006; Pizarro-Cerdá et al., 2017; Nolen et al., 2004; Nolen and Pollard, 2007; Espinoza-Sanchez et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: The main regulators of the ARP2/3 complex belong to the Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome protein (WASP) family proteins.
source: The main regulators of the ARP2/3 complex belong to the Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome protein (WASP) family proteins, including WASP-family verprolin-homologous protein (WAVE) (Yarar et al., 1999; Machesky et al., 1999; Higgs et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yarar et al., 1999; Machesky et al., 1999; Higgs et al., 1999.

claim: WASP and WAVE proteins serve as a link between the actin cytoskeleton and RhoGTPases via direct and intermediate binding to CDC42 and RAC1, respectively.
source: WASP and WAVE proteins serve as a link between the actin cytoskeleton and RhoGTPases via direct and intermediate binding to cell division control 42 (CDC42) and Ras-related C3 botulin toxin substrate 1 (RAC1), respectively (Rohatgi et al., 1999; Carlier et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rohatgi et al., 1999 and Carlier et al., 1999.

claim: The small RhoGTPases function as binary molecular switches circulating between active (GTP-bound) and inactive (GDP-bound) state.
source: They function as binary molecular switches circulating between active (GTP-bound) and inactive (GDP-bound) state.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about RhoGTPases.

claim: The on-off regulation of the RhoGTPases is under the control of guanine exchange factors (GEFs) and GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs).
source: The on-off regulation of the RhoGTPases is under the control of guanine exchange factors (GEFs) and GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) (Hodge and Ridley, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hodge and Ridley, 2016.

claim: GTP-bound active CDC42 and RAC1 promote the formation of filopodia and lamellipodia, respectively.
source: GTP-bound active CDC42 and RAC1 promote the formation of filopodia and lamellipodia, respectively, by activating the NPFs, WASP, and WAVE (Rohatgi et al., 1999; Carlier et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rohatgi et al., 1999 and Carlier et al., 1999.

claim: Recent studies revealed a role for kinases in directly activating RhoGTPases mainly through phosphorylation.
source: Recent studies revealed a role for kinases in directly activating RhoGTPases mainly through phosphorylation, but the identity of the relevant kinase(s) remained elusive (Tong et al., 2013; Forget et al., 2002; Chang et al., 2011; Tu et al., 2003; Ren et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to recent studies.

claim: ERK3 (MAPK6) is an atypical member of the mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPKs).
source: ERK3 (MAPK6) is an atypical member of the mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPKs).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about ERK3.

claim: Kinase-dependent roles of ERK3 include promoting lung cancer cell migration and invasion.
source: Its physiological roles are tissue-specific and can be both dependent and independent of its catalytic activity: kinase-dependent roles of ERK3 include promoting lung cancer cell migration and invasion, while its function in the regulation of breast cancer cell morphology and migration is shown to be partially kinase-independent (Al-Mahdi et al., 2015; Bogucka et al., 2021; Bogucka et al., 2020; Elkhadragy et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Al-Mahdi et al., 2015; Bogucka et al., 2021; Bogucka et al., 2020; Elkhadragy et al., 2020.

claim: ERK3's function in the regulation of breast cancer cell morphology and migration is shown to be partially kinase-independent.
source: Its physiological roles are tissue-specific and can be both dependent and independent of its catalytic activity: kinase-dependent roles of ERK3 include promoting lung cancer cell migration and invasion, while its function in the regulation of breast cancer cell morphology and migration is shown to be partially kinase-independent (Al-Mahdi et al., 2015; Bogucka et al., 2021; Bogucka et al., 2020; Elkhadragy et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Al-Mahdi et al., 2015; Bogucka et al., 2021; Bogucka et al., 2020; Elkhadragy et al., 2020.

claim: ERK3 is a labile protein whose rapid turnover has been implicated in cellular differentiation.
source: Moreover, ERK3 is a labile protein whose rapid turnover has been implicated in cellular differentiation (Bogucka et al., 2021; Coulombe et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bogucka et al., 2021 and Coulombe et al., 2003.

claim: ERK3 possesses a single phosphorylation site at serine 189 (S189) within S-E-G activation motif.
source: It is, however, known that ERK3 possesses a single phosphorylation site at serine 189 (S189) within S-E-G activation motif, located in its kinase domain, which was shown to be phosphorylated by group I p-21-activated kinases (PAKs), the direct effectors of RAC1 and CDC42 GTPases (Déléris et al., 2011; De la Mota-Peynado et al., 2011; Coulombe and Meloche, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Déléris et al., 2011; De la Mota-Peynado et al., 2011; Coulombe and Meloche, 2007.

claim: ERK3 signaling is required for the motility and migration of different cancer cells.
source: ERK3 signaling is required for the motility and migration of different cancer cells, yet its direct role in the regulation of the polarized phenotype of the cells and actin cytoskeleton is lacking.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from previous studies and the current work.

claim: Endogenous ERK3 co-localized to the F-actin-rich protrusions in human mammary epithelial cells (HMECs).
source: Endogenous ERK3 co-localized to the F-actin-rich protrusions in human mammary epithelial cells (HMECs) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemical data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Depletion of ERK3 reduced speed and displacement length of MDA-MB231 cells.
source: Depletion of ERK3 reduced speed and displacement length (distance between the start point and the end position of the cell along each axis) of MDA-MB231 cells (Figure 1B–F and Videos 1–4).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell tracking data shown in Figure 1B-F.

claim: Depletion of ERK3 strongly reduced random cell motility.
source: As shown in Figure 1C, depletion of ERK3 strongly reduced random cell motility, which remained low over time, as indicated by the calculated acceleration (Figure 1D) and concomitantly resulted in a shorter overall displacement length (Figure 1E) with shorter migration track length and average speed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell tracking data shown in Figure 1C-E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Intravital imaging of the orthotopic mammary tumors confirmed reduced motility of the ERK3 knockdown MDA-MB231-GFP cells.
source: Intravital imaging of the orthotopic mammary tumors confirmed reduced motility of the ERK3 knockdown MDA-MB231-GFP cells (Figure 1G and Videos 5 and 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by intravital imaging data shown in Figure 1G and Videos 5 and 6.

claim: Knockdown of ERK3 significantly attenuated the EGF-induced chemotaxis of both HMECs and metastatic MDA-MB231 cells.
source: Interestingly, knockdown of ERK3 significantly attenuated the EGF-induced chemotaxis of both cell types (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by chemotaxis assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-F.

claim: EGF induced serine 189 (S189) phosphorylation of ERK3 at early time points in primary epithelial cells.
source: EGF induced serine 189 (S189) phosphorylation of ERK3 at early time points in primary epithelial cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B) and MDA-MB231 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-D.

claim: EGF treatment did not increase ERK3 protein half-life.
source: Further cycloheximide (CHX) chase experiments coupled with RT-PCR analyses suggested that EGF treatment did not increase ERK3 protein half-life (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E–2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by CHX chase and RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E-2H.

claim: Knockdown of ERK3 clearly reduced F-actin content and actin-rich protrusions in human mammary primary epithelial cells.
source: Moreover, knockdown of ERK3 clearly reduced F-actin content and actin-rich protrusions in human mammary primary epithelial cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: ERK3-depleted cells had limited, diffuse F-actin, concentrated in the cortical areas of the cells, and a significantly decreased number of filopodia.
source: Further analyses of control and ERK3 knockdown HMECs at the single-cell level confirmed that ERK3-depleted cells had limited, diffuse F-actin, concentrated in the cortical areas of the cells, and a significantly decreased number of filopodia (Figure 1G–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal and SEM imaging data shown in Figure 1G-J.

claim: EGF signaling triggers activation of RAC1 and CDC42.
source: EGF signaling triggers activation of RAC1 and CDC42, which link the signal to the actin cytoskeleton leading to the formation of lamellipodia- and filopodia-like protrusions, respectively (Figure 2A; Kurokawa et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kurokawa et al., 2004 and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: ERK3 knockdown significantly decreased the levels of both basal and EGF-induced GTP-bound CDC42 and RAC1 in primary (HMEC) and triple-negative breast cancer (MDA-MB231) mammary epithelial cells.
source: ERK3 knockdown significantly decreased the levels of both basal and EGF-induced GTP-bound CDC42 and RAC1 in primary (HMEC) (Figure 2B, D, and F) and triple-negative breast cancer (MDA-MB231) mammary epithelial cells (Figure 2C, E, and G), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 2B-G.

claim: ERK3 protein co-precipitated with the active RhoGTPases at endogenous levels.
source: Intriguingly, we could observe co-precipitation of ERK3 protein with the active RhoGTPases at endogenous levels, suggesting that these proteins exist in a multimeric complex (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Depletion of ERK3 reduced the activity of RAC1 and CDC42 in multiple cell types.
source: We expanded these analyses to different cell types and consistently found that depletion of ERK3 reduced the activity of RAC1 and CDC42 and that the active RhoGTPases specifically co-precipitated endogenous ERK3 (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: ERK3 directly bound to RAC1 and CDC42 in a nucleotide-independent manner.
source: By employing purified full-length recombinant proteins, we found that ERK3 directly bound to RAC1 and CDC42 in a nucleotide-independent manner (Figure 2H and I).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro GST pull-down data shown in Figure 2H and I.

claim: Binding of full-length ERK3 to RAC1 and CDC42 could be detected at a low nanomolar range (5 nM).
source: Binding of full-length ERK3 to RAC1 and CDC42 could be detected at a low nanomolar range (5 nM) (Figure 2J and K).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2J and K.

claim: The kinase domain of ERK3 was sufficient for its binding to RAC1 and CDC42.
source: In vitro GST-pull-down assays confirmed that the kinase domain of ERK3 was sufficient for its binding to RAC1 and CDC42 (Figure 2L and Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by GST pull-down data shown in Figure 2L and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The ERK3 kinase domain stimulated GDP-GTP exchange on CDC42.
source: These experiments showed that although ERK3 regulated the activity of both CDC42 and RAC1 in cultured cells, it only directly stimulated the GDP-GTP exchange of CDC42 (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro GDP-GTP exchange assay data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: ERK3 did not directly stimulate the GDP-GTP exchange of RAC1.
source: These experiments showed that although ERK3 regulated the activity of both CDC42 and RAC1 in cultured cells, it only directly stimulated the GDP-GTP exchange of CDC42 (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro GDP-GTP exchange assay data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Addition of ERK3 stimulated GTP-loading on CDC42 in a fluorophore-based assay.
source: The results confirmed those of the previous assay as addition of ERK3 stimulated GTP-loading on CDC42 (Figure 3F) but not on RAC1 (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorophore-based GEF activity assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: ERK3 exerted a more potent and long-lasting effect than Dbl's Big Sister (Dbs) on CDC42 activation.
source: Notably, ERK3 exerted a more potent and long-lasting effect than Dbl's Big Sister (Dbs), a well-established GEF for CDC42 and RhoA proteins (Figure 3F; Baumeister et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorophore-based GEF activity assay data shown in Figure 3F and a citation to Baumeister et al., 2006.

claim: Full-length ERK3 exhibited weaker GEF activity in vitro than the kinase domain of ERK3.
source: Interestingly, full-length ERK3 exhibited weaker GEF activity in vitro than the kinase domain of ERK3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by GEF activity assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Knockdown of ERK3 does not disrupt the localization of CDC42 and RAC1 to the plasma membrane.
source: Cellular fractionation assays revealed that knockdown of ERK3 does not disrupt the localization of CDC42 and RAC1 to the PM (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cellular fractionation data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: The plasma membrane fraction from ERK3-depleted HMECs had more total CDC42 and RAC1 than control cells.
source: On the contrary, the PM fraction from ERK3-depleted HMECs had more total CDC42 and RAC1 than control cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by cellular fractionation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Although both RhoGTPases are present at the plasma membrane in the absence of ERK3, their activity is significantly reduced.
source: Interestingly, subsequent pull-down of active CDC42/RAC1 from the PM fraction revealed that although both RhoGTPases are present at the plasma membrane in the absence of ERK3, their activity is significantly reduced (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by pull-down assay data from plasma membrane fractions shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: ERK3 colocalized with CDC42 to the protrusions at the leading edge of the cell.
source: These results were corroborated by the colocalization of ERK3 with CDC42 to the protrusions at the leading edge of the cell (Figure 4D–G) with mean Pearson's correlation coefficient (PCC (r)) of 0.6638 ± 0.02946 and Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (SRCC (ρ)): 0.7122 ± 0.02586 (Figure 4F and G, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and colocalization analysis data shown in Figure 4D-G.

claim: ARP2/3 complex subunits ARP3, ARP2, and ARPC1A co-precipitated with active RAC1/CDC42 along with ERK3.
source: Interestingly, we readily detected the ARP2/3 complex subunits ARP3, ARP2, and ARPC1A, as well as ERK3 by immunoblots in active RAC1/CDC42 pull-downs (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Knockdown of ERK3 by CRISPR/Cas9 or with si/shRNAs led to a reduction in F-actin staining in mammary epithelial cells.
source: Consistent with the reduction in active RAC1 and CDC42 levels, we observed that knockdown of ERK3 by CRISPR/Cas9 or with si/shRNAs led to a reduction in F-actin staining in mammary epithelial cells as shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Knockdown of ERK3 significantly shifted total F-actin to G-actin in both primary HMECs and MDA-MB231 cancer cells.
source: Knockdown of ERK3 significantly shifted total F-actin to G-actin in both primary HMECs (Figure 5D and E) and MDA-MB231 cancer cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by F/G-actin assay data shown in Figure 5D-E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: In the absence of CDC42, colocalization between endogenous ERK3 and the ARP3 subunit of the ARP2/3 complex could still be detected.
source: Moreover, in the absence of CDC42, we could still detect colocalization between endogenous ERK3 and the ARP3 subunit of the ARP2/3 complex (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and colocalization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-D.

claim: Recombinant ERK3 stimulated ARP2/3-dependent actin polymerization at a nanomolar concentration (5 nM) in the presence of 10 nM of the ARP2/3 complex.
source: Indeed, recombinant ERK3 stimulated ARP2/3-dependent actin polymerization at a nanomolar concentration (5 nM) in the presence of 10 nM of the ARP2/3 complex (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by pyrene-actin polymerization assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The nucleation-promoting activity of ERK3 was comparable to WASP (VCA).
source: Moreover, the nucleation-promoting activity of ERK3 was comparable to WASP (VCA), a well-known NPF.
evidence: The claim is supported by pyrene-actin polymerization assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: ERK3 protein alone did not exert any stimulatory effect on actin nucleation.
source: ERK3 protein alone did not exert any stimulatory effect on actin nucleation (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by pyrene-actin polymerization assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Full-length ERK3 bound to the ARP2/3 complex with high-affinity in vitro.
source: Indeed, using quantitative ELISAs we found that full-length ERK3 bound to the ARP2/3 complex with high-affinity in vitro (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: ERK3 directly binds to ARP3 in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: Through GST pull-down experiments with purified recombinant proteins, we could indeed detect a concentration-dependent direct binding between full-length ERK3 and ARP3 (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by GST pull-down data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Full-length ERK3 binds to ARP3 with high affinity.
source: These results were further confirmed with ELISA analyses suggesting a high-affinity binding between these two proteins (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: ERK3 co-precipitated with ARP3 and ARP2 in HMECs at endogenous levels.
source: Finally, we also detected ERK3 co-precipitating with ARP3 and ARP2 in HMECs at endogenous levels (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Phosphorylation of ARP3 at serine 418 (S418) was detected by mass spectrometry after in vitro kinase assay with ERK3.
source: Initial analyses detected phosphorylation of the ARP3 subunit at serine 418 (S418) (peptide sequence: HNPVFGVMS, please see Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data after in vitro kinase assay.

claim: Expression of the phosphorylation-mimicking ARP3 mutant (S418D) predominantly induced actin filament formation.
source: Strikingly, expression of the phosphorylation-mimicking ARP3 mutant (S418D) under these settings predominantly induced actin filament formation, as indicated by the intense phalloidin staining (Figure 6F) and enhanced the F/G-actin ratio in primary mammary epithelial cells (Figure 6I and J).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and F/G-actin assay data shown in Figure 6F, I, and J.

claim: S418D-overexpressing cells exhibited F-actin-rich protrusions.
source: Moreover, S418D-overexpressing cells exhibited F-actin-rich protrusions (Figure 6F, lower panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Cells expressing non-phosphorylatable ARP3 (ARP3 S418A) had no significant effect on overall F-actin levels.
source: Quantification of the F-actin levels revealed that despite the morphological distortion, cells expressing non-phosphorylatable ARP3 (ARP3 S418A) had no significant effect on overall F-actin levels (Figure 6I and J).
evidence: The claim is supported by F/G-actin assay data shown in Figure 6I and J.

claim: Knockdown of ERK3 led to a significant reduction of the F-actin levels in the ARP3 S418D-overexpressing cells.
source: Knockdown of ERK3 led to a significant reduction of the F-actin levels in the ARP3 S418D-overexpressing cells (Figure 6K–M).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and F/G-actin assay data shown in Figure 6K-M.

claim: Knockdown of ERK3 in ARP3 S418D-overexpressing cells revealed a significant decrease in RAC1 activity, with almost no effect on CDC42.
source: A concomitant active RAC1/CDC42 pull-down revealed a significant decrease in RAC1 activity, with almost no effect on CDC42 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Significant colocalization between endogenous ERK3 and ARP3 was observed in HMECs.
source: Using immunofluorescence analysis, we observed significant colocalization between endogenous ERK3 and ARP3 in HMECs (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and colocalization data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Depletion of ERK3 reduced the migration of ARP3 S418D-expressing cells.
source: Further, depletion of ERK3, as expected, reduced the migration of ARP3 S418D-expressing cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by Transwell migration assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2G and H.

claim: Knockdown of ERK3 led to a decrease in actin-rich protrusions and overall F-actin staining.
source: Knockdown of ERK3 led to a decrease in actin-rich protrusions and overall F-actin staining (Figure 7B) with concomitant decrease in F-actin abundance (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and F/G-actin assay data shown in Figure 7B-D.

claim: Complementation with ERK3 WT rescued overall F-actin levels and the protrusive phenotype of the HMECs.
source: Complementation with ERK3 WT rescued overall F-actin levels and the protrusive phenotype of the HMECs (Figure 7B and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and F/G-actin assay data shown in Figure 7B and D.

claim: KD ERK3 recovered cytoskeletal F-actin levels to the same extent as ERK3 WT.
source: Interestingly, KD ERK3 recovered cytoskeletal F-actin levels to the same extent as ERK3 WT (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by F/G-actin assay data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: Although the abundance of F-actin is rescued upon KD ERK3 overexpression, cells formed a dense meshwork of actin membrane ruffles which did not protrude into filopodia.
source: However, although the abundance of F-actin is rescued upon KD ERK3 overexpression, cells formed a dense meshwork of actin membrane ruffles which did not protrude into filopodia but rather curved around the edges of the cell forming a tangled web (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Kinase activity of ERK3 did not seem to affect the ARP2/3-dependent actin polymerization in vitro.
source: Kinase activity of ERK3 did not seem to affect the ARP2/3-dependent actin polymerization in vitro (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by pyrene-actin polymerization assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The kinase activity of ERK3 was not required for interactions or activation of CDC42.
source: We performed active RAC1/CDC42 pull-down from HMECs shERK3 (3′ UTR) cells reconstituted with either WT or the KD ERK3 and found that the kinase activity of ERK3 was not required for interactions or activation of CDC42.
evidence: The claim is supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 7E-I.

claim: RAC1 activation was partially dependent on the kinase activity of ERK3.
source: However, RAC1 activation was partially dependent on the kinase activity of ERK3 (Figure 7E–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 7E-I.

claim: ERK3 has been shown to regulate mammary epithelial cancer cell migration and metastasis.
source: ERK3 has been shown to regulate mammary epithelial cancer cell migration and metastasis (Al-Mahdi et al., 2015; Bogucka et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Al-Mahdi et al., 2015 and Bogucka et al., 2020.

claim: Reorganization of actin protrusions at the leading edge of the cells initiates cell migration.
source: Reorganization of actin protrusions at the leading edge of the cells initiates cell migration (Yamaguchi and Condeelis, 2007; Affolter and Weijer, 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yamaguchi and Condeelis, 2007 and Affolter and Weijer, 2005.

claim: In response to extracellular guidance, cells polarize and extend F-actin-rich protrusions at the leading edge to direct cell migration.
source: In response to extracellular guidance, cells polarize and extend F-actin-rich protrusions at the leading edge to direct cell migration (Affolter and Weijer, 2005; Ridley et al., 2003; Lauffenburger and Horwitz, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Affolter and Weijer, 2005; Ridley et al., 2003; Lauffenburger and Horwitz, 1996.

claim: RhoGTPases are the major membrane signaling transmitters that drive polarized cell asymmetry by locally regulating the formation of F-actin-rich protrusions.
source: RhoGTPases are the major membrane signaling transmitters that drive polarized cell asymmetry by locally regulating the formation of F-actin-rich protrusions (Hall, 1998; Nobes and Hall, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hall, 1998 and Nobes and Hall, 1995.

claim: Active RAC1 and CDC42 induce ARP2/3-dependent actin polymerization by activating their effector NPFs, WASP and WAVE, respectively.
source: Active RAC1 and CDC42 induce ARP2/3-dependent actin polymerization by activating their effector NPFs, WASP and WAVE, respectively (Rohatgi et al., 1999; Carlier et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rohatgi et al., 1999 and Carlier et al., 1999.

claim: ARP2 and ARP3 are essential for the nucleating activity of the ARP2/3 complex and occupy the central position in actin nucleation.
source: ARP2 and ARP3 are essential for the nucleating activity of the ARP2/3 complex and occupy the central position in actin nucleation.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the ARP2/3 complex.

claim: ARP3 is crucial for the stimulation and activity of the ARP2/3 complex and nucleation in vitro.
source: Extensive characterization of the individual subunits also revealed that ARP3 is crucial for the stimulation and activity of the ARP2/3 complex and nucleation in vitro (Gournier et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gournier et al., 2001.

claim: Conformational changes activating ARP2/3 are induced by binding to NPFs, actin, and ATP.
source: Conformational changes activating ARP2/3 are induced by binding to NPFs, actin, and ATP.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about ARP2/3 activation.

claim: Phosphorylation of various ARP2/3 residues has been reported previously to play a crucial role in the conformational rearrangements within the ARP2/3 complex.
source: Additionally, phosphorylation of various ARP2/3 residues has been reported previously to play a crucial role in the conformational rearrangements within the ARP2/3 complex (Vadlamudi et al., 2004; Singh et al., 2003; Narayanan et al., 2011; LeClaire et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Vadlamudi et al., 2004; Singh et al., 2003; Narayanan et al., 2011; LeClaire et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2013.

claim: ARP3, ARP2 and ARPC1A purified from Acanthamoeba castellani were shown to be phosphorylated.
source: From the seven components of the ARP2/3 complex ARP3, ARP2 and ARPC1A purified from Acanthamoeba castellani were shown to be phosphorylated (LeClaire et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to LeClaire et al., 2008.

claim: Phosphorylation at S418 of ARP3 promoted actin polymerization and thus the F-actin content.
source: These data suggested that although phosphorylation at S418 of ARP3 promoted actin polymerization and thus the F-actin content it is not absolutely essential like ERK3.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from ARP3 mutant overexpression experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Kinase activity of ERK3 is not required for the polymerization of actin, but rather for the bundling and/or branching of the rapidly polymerizing actin filaments.
source: These results indicate that kinase activity of ERK3 is not required for the polymerization of actin, but rather for the bundling and/or branching of the rapidly polymerizing actin filaments.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from complementation experiments with kinase-dead ERK3 shown in Figure 7.

claim: PAK family kinases, the effector kinases of RAC1 and CDC42, directly phosphorylate the SEG motif in the activation loop of ERK3.
source: It is highly interesting that PAK family kinases, the effector kinases of RAC1 and CDC42, directly phosphorylate the SEG motif in the activation loop of ERK3 (Déléris et al., 2011; De la Mota-Peynado et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Déléris et al., 2011 and De la Mota-Peynado et al., 2011.

claim: ERK3 is required for the GTP loading of CDC42 and RAC1 to induce their interaction with PAKs, which in turn phosphorylate and activate ERK3.
source: The observations presented here strongly suggest a positive feedback loop, where ERK3 is required for the GTP loading of CDC42 and RAC1 to induce their interaction with PAKs, which in turn phosphorylate and activate ERK3.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data and established knowledge about PAK-ERK3 interactions.

claim: Active ERK3 kinase is required for the eventual formation of actin-regulated membrane protrusions.
source: We show that active ERK3 kinase is required for the eventual formation of actin-regulated membrane protrusions.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from complementation experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Regulatory pathways involved in the filopodia formation seem to be cell type-specific.
source: To complicate matters further, regulatory pathways involved in the filopodia formation seem to be cell type-specific, and CDC42-, WASP-, and ARP2/3-independent mechanisms of membrane spikes formation have been proposed (Czuchra et al., 2005; Snapper et al., 2001; Steffen et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Czuchra et al., 2005; Snapper et al., 2001; Steffen et al., 2006.

claim: Phosphorylation of certain subunits of ARP2/3 complex has been shown to be indispensable for the destabilization of its inactive conformation prior the full activation by the NPFs.
source: Interestingly, phosphorylation of certain subunits of ARP2/3 complex has been shown to be indispensable for the destabilization of its inactive conformation prior the full activation by the NPFs (Vadlamudi et al., 2004; Narayanan et al., 2011; LeClaire et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Vadlamudi et al., 2004; Narayanan et al., 2011; LeClaire et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2013.

claim: Nck-interacting kinase (NIK) regulates ARP2 phosphorylation and grooms the ARP2/3 complex for the activation by NPFs.
source: LeClaire et al. further reported that Nck-interacting kinase (NIK) regulates ARP2 phosphorylation and grooms the ARP2/3 complex for the activation by NPFs.
evidence: The claim is supported by a reference to LeClaire et al.'s work.

claim: ERK3 binding to ARP2/3 and possibly other hitherto unknown factors per se contribute to actin polymerization.
source: These data suggest that perhaps ERK3 binding to ARP2/3 and possibly other hitherto unknown factors per se contribute to actin polymerization, while its kinase activity is probably still required for ARP2/3-dependent and CDC42-induced filopodia formation, polarization, and migration of mammalian epithelial cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing kinase-independent effects on F-actin levels.

claim: ERK3 kinase activity is probably still required for ARP2/3-dependent and CDC42-induced filopodia formation, polarization, and migration of mammalian epithelial cells.
source: These data suggest that perhaps ERK3 binding to ARP2/3 and possibly other hitherto unknown factors per se contribute to actin polymerization, while its kinase activity is probably still required for ARP2/3-dependent and CDC42-induced filopodia formation, polarization, and migration of mammalian epithelial cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing kinase-dependent effects on protrusion formation.

claim: ERK3 is druggable, and kinase inhibitors have already been developed for clinical use.
source: ERK3 is druggable, and kinase inhibitors have already been developed for clinical use, which could also serve as tools to decipher kinase-dependent and -independent functions.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge about kinase inhibitors.
